title: 3D modeling questions Viking 'fast fashion'
summary: High-resolution 3D modeling of Viking brooches and the molds used to make them identifies surprisingly few matches between them, indicating the brooches were not mass-produced, as previously thought, but instead made by individual, creative artisans.

title: AI could be used to write your child's report. Is this a problem?
summary: For many families, it's that time of year when school reports land in parents' inboxes.

title: AI simulates electron hops over far longer times than conventional quantum calculations
summary: To predict how a material will behave, we need to know which atoms are located where. This allows us, for example, to explain whether a material is suitable as a catalyst for certain chemical reactions. But often, that is not enough: even if all the atoms stay exactly where they are, the distribution of electric charge within the material can change dramatically. Electrons can jump from one atom to another, changing the forces between atoms as well as the material's chemical reactivity.

title: Is AI‑assisted thinking devaluing business degrees?
summary: As AI models improve, high-quality knowledge is becoming easier to access. A degree therefore has to certify something more durable than the ability to retrieve knowledge or produce a plausible answer. It must show that a student can exercise judgment, make decisions and defend them.

title: How ancient builders helped the Lighthouse of Alexandria withstand 18 earthquakes
summary: More than 2,000 years after it was built, the legendary Lighthouse of Alexandria is being brought back to life through scientific research and the use of virtual universes. For the first time, a scientifically complete 3D reconstruction reveals how one of the Seven Wonders of the World was built.

title: Antarctic sea ice extent hits new low
summary: Satellite observations show Antarctic sea ice coverage dipped to record daily lows in October 2026, surpassing even the extremely low extent observed in October 2023—the year poor sea ice conditions led to the deaths of thousands of emperor penguin chicks in Antarctica.

title: New atlas unites nearly 3,500 laser surveys to map forests across 56 countries
summary: An international team of researchers led by the University of Bristol in the U.K. has unveiled the Global Canopy Atlas—the largest integrated collection of high-resolution 3D maps of forests, woodlands and savannas ever assembled.

title: Bacterial colonies turn themselves inside out when oxygen is scarce
summary: Bacteria can protect themselves from external threats by forming colonies. The physical principles that govern the structure of such colonies, and in particular their structural transformations, are poorly understood.

title: When bad weather hits a fragile financial system
summary: An extreme weather event does more than just destroy buildings, facilities or infrastructure. It can also reduce the value of collateral, weaken banks, make credit more expensive and force businesses to postpone investment. Consequently, the damage risks spreading well beyond the locality where the event occurred.

title: Melting Barents Sea ice gives Eastern Europe's farmers a spring boost
summary: For decades, sea ice in the Barents Sea, a part of the Arctic Ocean north of Norway and Russia, has been shrinking as the Arctic warms. The loss of so much ice can alter weather patterns well beyond the polar region, including in Europe. But how these changes might affect vegetation growth and agricultural production is less well understood.

title: Battery-free implant harvests ultrasound energy and glows to reveal its condition
summary: Implantable bioelectronics enable health care professionals to continuously monitor patients' physiological conditions, deliver targeted treatments and support recovery. However, once implanted, these devices are difficult to inspect directly, and damage or degradation may go undetected until complications occur. Limited battery lifetimes and leakage risks also raise safety concerns.

title: Beeswax and pine link crocodile mummies made centuries apart at one Egyptian site
summary: In a practice spanning centuries, ancient Egyptians mummified thousands of crocodiles they associated with Sobek, a god linked to the Nile, fertility and royal power. In one unique example, embalmers from the middle of the 1st millennium BC at Kom Ombo in southern Egypt mounted more than 25 hatchlings on reeds along the back and neck of a crocodile nearly 4 meters (13 feet) long. The arrangement may echo the way young crocodiles ride on their mother's back.

title: Researchers call for a better understanding of who benefits from new green space
summary: Parks, woodlands, rivers and other natural spaces can improve physical and mental health, encourage exercise and help cities cope with extreme heat and flooding—but simply creating more green spaces does not guarantee that everyone will benefit equally.

title: Brazil loses up to 75 days of rainy season as extreme heat threatens food production
summary: Parts of Brazil have lost up to 75 days of their rainy season over the past three decades, while extreme heat is becoming increasingly common across millions of hectares of farmland, according to new research involving The University of Manchester.

title: Bushfire disaster ignites citizen science tourism
summary: The devastating Black Summer wildfires on Kangaroo Island accelerated interest in citizen science tourism—a movement gaining momentum as climate-related disasters place unprecedented pressure on native species and landscapes.

title: Carbon storage wells linked to earthquakes near Canadian city
summary: People across Edmonton, Canada, felt the ground shake on April 1 and again on May 9, 2026. After the May quake, the Alberta Energy Regulator said it had received no reports of damage or injuries. Researchers have now traced both earthquakes to carbon dioxide injected at Alberta's Quest storage project.

title: 'That's when the chaos began': The fall of the Berlin Wall in the words of East and West Germans
summary: Germany's far right is on the rise, with current polls suggesting the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has the backing of 28% of voters nationally. This makes it the most popular party in the country, ahead of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats at 20%.

title: Constantly following war-related news can cause worry and anxiety
summary: "If a student is very confident about their ability to cope even in difficult situations, following war-related news will not cause them much anxiety. Confidence in one's ability to cope can therefore help protect against the psychological distress associated with various crises—in this case, distress linked to following war-related news," says Taina Hintsa, professor of health psychology.

title: Targeted conversion of carbon dioxide into chemical feedstocks: CO₂ helps shape its own catalyst
summary: Electrochemists at the University of Duisburg-Essen have discovered through computer simulations that carbon dioxide (CO₂) helps shape the surface of its own catalyst when the catalyst is restructured using voltage pulses. The calculations suggest that this allows CO₂ to be converted preferentially into formic acid. The findings have been published in Advanced Functional Materials.

title: Cosmology technique inspires better characterization of ocean swirls and waves
summary: A new study from Caltech uses a mathematical framework borrowed from cosmology to analyze ocean data and characterize individual flow features in the churning chaos. With the technique, the researchers are able to measure and characterize features in maps of the ocean surface, allowing them to differentiate ocean flows that otherwise look identical when evaluated with standard analysis tools.

title: Study finds lasting changes in daily mobility patterns across Latin America after COVID-19
summary: Researchers at the University of Liverpool have used anonymized Facebook mobility data to explore how everyday movement patterns changed across Latin American countries in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Decoding how fish adapt to varying salt concentrations
summary: Freshwater and seawater fishes face different challenges in maintaining the balance of salts and water in their bodies. To survive these changing conditions, they rely on specialized transport proteins in organs like the kidneys and intestine to regulate electrolyte transport. However, important questions regarding the molecular mechanisms that support salt transport and acclimatization to different environmental salinities persist.

title: Denisovan remains and an unknown archaic human lineage discovered in southern China
summary: An international team of researchers, including first author Song Xing, a researcher affiliated with the Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana (CENIEH), has just published a study in the journal Nature that analyzed four fossil teeth recovered from two caves in southern China. The team has identified two possible human lineages dating to the Middle and Late Pleistocene: one with Denisovan affinities and another more primitive lineage whose evolutionary identity remains unclear.

title: Digital access to early music
summary: What may look to modern readers like a form of secret code in fact opens the door to a fascinating world of historical music: German lute tablature. Developed specifically for the Renaissance lute, this rich notational tradition preserves dances, songs and other musical works that were immensely popular some 500 years ago. As part of an interdisciplinary team of experts, researchers at the University of Bayreuth are now making these sources readable and audible once again through a digital scholarly edition platform.

title: Dolly Parton gets a deep-sea namesake: Bathyadmetella dollypartonae
summary: A "beautiful" new species from one of the least-known areas of the ocean has been named after Dolly Parton. Scientists at the Natural History Museum work 9 to 5, and more besides, to name dozens of marine species every year. So, when they identified a new species of worm covered in pale, hairlike sheaths, there was only one choice for whom to name it after—and it wasn't Jolene.

title: Using a drone and a poop-sniffing dog, scientists perform health checks on endangered orcas
summary: Every fall for the last few years, Deborah Giles starts her workday with one question in mind: Where are the orcas?

title: Drones offer a new view of wildlife health. But what are they missing?
summary: Drones are transforming how scientists study wildlife, allowing researchers to photograph and measure animals in their natural environments, monitor larger populations and collect observations with less disturbance. While a photograph can reveal changes in an animal's size and shape, it cannot confidently tell researchers what those changes mean for its health.

title: The first flash of a dying star can reveal its hidden surroundings
summary: When a massive star dies, the universe does not always announce it with the familiar, slowly expanding glow of a supernova. Its very first signal can be a dazzling, short-lived flash of invisible light—a cosmic camera flash that lasts only hours. That fleeting moment offers an unusually direct glimpse of the star at the instant of destruction. But what if the light has to fight its way through a cloud of gas the star expelled before dying?

title: European oil and gas firms likely downplayed energy crisis profits, study finds
summary: Following the Russian attack on Ukraine in February 2022, energy costs rose sharply and many households and businesses felt the financial burden immediately. Oil and gas companies, however, were making extraordinary profits during this time. As public criticism of high energy costs grew, how did these companies handle their profits? A new study shows that European oil and gas firms likely downplayed their profits between 2022 and 2023. These earnings management practices were particularly prevalent in countries that introduced windfall profit taxes as well as in countries with strong democratic institutions.

title: The faintest supernova ever observed refuses to go out, staying visible for nearly a year
summary: An international team of astronomers, including Paul Groot of Radboud University, has discovered that a supernova explosion does not always have to be extremely bright. The team has identified the faintest supernova observed to date. It remained visible for an exceptionally long time and appears to have been caused by a so-called white dwarf and a relatively small companion star. The discovery may have implications for our understanding of the evolution of binary stars and the measurement of the expansion of the universe. The results were published in Nature Astronomy.

title: Familiar faces help children develop emotional understanding
summary: Across two studies, researchers from Adelaide University, the University of Queensland and Victoria University of Wellington studied parents' and children's recognition of emotional expressions.

title: Why fertile male killifish outlive their peers
summary: Why do some individuals of the same species live significantly longer than others? In evolutionary biology and aging research, this question is often linked to a trade-off between reproduction and survival. The underlying idea is that energy and resources invested in reproduction may lead to compromises in repair and maintenance, thereby hindering a long life. Thus, the assumption is that particularly successful reproduction at a young age comes at the cost of a shorter lifespan.

title: Fiber-optic sensing unearths surprising complexity in small California earthquake
summary: More than 20,000 earthquakes are located worldwide each year, but the vast majority of those are small—many too small to be felt by humans. Scientists have historically assumed most of these small earthquakes break as small, circular ruptures in which the rocks in a fault slip past each other in a single, smooth motion, and the crack spreads outward from one point like a ripple in a pond, unlike the behavior of most major earthquakes.

title: New research establishes fundamental complexity limit for quantum circuit optimization
summary: Quantum circuit optimization is an important research area, as the computational resources required to execute quantum algorithms remain a major challenge. In particular, two-qubit operations are generally associated with higher error rates than single-qubit gates on current quantum hardware, making reducing the number of two-qubit gates an important objective.

title: Hera reveals stadium-sized asteroid crater from spacecraft impact
summary: Arriving at the site of humankind's first planetary defense experiment, the European Space Agency's Hera mission has found a miniature world of surprises. Dimorphos—the small asteroid whose orbit around a second, larger asteroid was deflected by a spacecraft impact—now has one face flattened with a stadium-sized crater and is tumbling chaotically. Meanwhile, hundreds of previously unknown boulders encircle the binary pair.

title: Could a hidden planet twice Earth's mass explain strange orbits beyond Neptune?
summary: In the cold, dark Kuiper belt region beyond Neptune, some icy bodies travel on steeply tilted paths, while others stay far from the giant planets even at their closest approach to the sun. A simulation study suggests that a hidden planet about twice Earth's mass could help explain both populations of objects.

title: Income inequality is rising while becoming more similar across countries
summary: Inequality is a much-debated issue in politics and society. International comparative research shows that income inequality has risen in most countries. At the same time, however, the differences in disposable income levels between countries have narrowed.

title: Internet cables double as seismic sensors to map earthquake faults in fine detail
summary: Along the rugged spine of New Zealand's South Island lies the Alpine Fault, a major tectonic boundary between the Australian and Pacific plates. The fault last unleashed a major earthquake in 1717, and geoscientists estimate a 75% probability of a rupture of magnitude 7 or greater occurring within the next 50 years.

title: Lab experiments suggest bat RSV can enter human cells, but existing antibodies block it
summary: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes severe respiratory disease and is responsible for numerous deaths each year. A research team led by DZIF scientist Dr. Wendy K. Jo and DZIF scientist Dr. Jan Felix Drexler at Charité—University Medicine Berlin, as well as DZIF board member Dr. Thomas Pietschmann and Dr. Sibylle Haid from TWINCORE in Hanover, has now characterized a virus in West African fruit bats that is genetically distinct from known RSV variants but belongs to the same viral family as RSV.

title: The structure of large corporations changes the rules of innovation
summary: Why do two large multinationals operating in the same industry choose completely different organizational structures? And why are some subsidiaries in direct contact with the parent company, while others are separated from the top by numerous hierarchical levels?

title: Rocks under the lens: A simple microscope opens new possibilities for quantitative rock analysis
summary: Rocks hold a wealth of information about Earth's history. The size, shape and orientation of the mineral grains that make them up can reveal how rocks formed, deformed and changed deep beneath the surface. However, collecting this information has traditionally required specialized equipment and time-consuming analysis.

title: Work-life balance predicts job satisfaction more strongly than pay or flexible working in study
summary: Work-life balance has a stronger association with job satisfaction than pay or flexible working arrangements, according to a study of employees in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) published in the International Journal of Economics and Business Research.

title: Lizards build complex teeth differently from humans
summary: Researchers from the Institute of Biotechnology, part of the Helsinki Institute of Life Science (HiLIFE) at the University of Helsinki, have shown how evolution can produce similarly complex tooth shapes through very different biological mechanisms.

title: How mammals zigzagged their way to modern posture
summary: This is the story of how mammals came to dominate the Earth—and the crooked evolutionary path they trod en route. Early mammals and their ancestors left behind fossilized bones, footprints and lots of questions about how they moved. One key element of their evolutionary saga involved how these four-legged creatures shifted from what researchers call a "sprawled" stance, with limbs splayed like lizards, to more "erect" postures, with limbs directly beneath the body, that allowed for more speed and agility.

title: Meteor blast scars hint at Venus's gradual volcanic makeover
summary: In a radar image from NASA's Magellan spacecraft, a dark spot about 20 kilometers (12 miles) wide sits inside two bright halos on Venus (see images C and D above). The fainter outer halo spans some 180 kilometers (110 miles), yet there is no obvious crater at the center. A space rock may have created the entire pattern by exploding in the planet's thick atmosphere.

title: Newly discovered barrier could explain why nucleic acid medicines remain trapped inside cells
summary: Researchers from the Department of Chemistry at The University of Hong Kong (HKU) and their collaborators have discovered a barrier that may prevent some promising nucleic acid medicines from reaching their targets inside subcellular compartments. Published in Nature Cell Biology, the findings could help guide the development of more effective drug delivery strategies.

title: Nonlinear optical lattice boosts spatial coherence by concentrating light in a single mode
summary: Light waves can have varying degrees of coherence, which means that the consistency of the relationship between their phases across space or time can differ. Reliable methods to enhance the coherence of light could pave the way for the development of high-quality lasers and scientific instruments.

title: What are the odds of a volcano erupting through a salt lake?
summary: An experimental study of what happens when volcanoes erupt through salt lakes is rewriting the genesis story on the formation of some iron ore and rare earth deposits. The Australian National University (ANU) research looks beyond common assumptions, reconciling decades of research. The findings indicate that the various proposed mineral formation routes, or genesis pathways, are not necessarily mutually exclusive.

title: Measuring surprise in online attention
summary: The difference between attention and surprise matters when public-interest forecasts guide media planning or decisions about the capacity needed to handle traffic. The paper, presented at the IEEE Technology and Engineering Management Society Conference (TEMSCON LATAM) in Quito, Ecuador, in June 2026, provides a common statistical approach for following changes in attention and forecast errors separately.

title: New educational program developed for an often-overlooked group of gifted children
summary: Pupils from families with a lower socio-economic status (SES) perform less well at school than children from families with a high socio-economic status. They are also less likely to be identified as gifted pupils. Ph.D. candidate Lineke van Tricht has developed a program for schools to help pupils with a low SES make the most of their talents. "This is important for the young people themselves, but also for society as a whole," says Van Tricht, who will defend her thesis at Radboud University on 8 December 2026.

title: Study shows path to more resilient future for Canada's forests
summary: Mountain pine beetles have killed millions of lodgepole pines across western North America since the 1990s, but some trees have proved more resilient than others. New research suggests part of the difference is genetic and that the resistance can be passed from one generation of trees to the next.

title: Q&A: What matters most to homeowners facing flooding?
summary: The annual amount of precipitation and the frequency of extreme events have increased in Pennsylvania in recent decades, and both are expected to continue increasing, leading to a higher flood risk. Most climate risk studies, however, reflect a limited understanding of how people interpret and act on flood risk. To develop a stronger culture of proactive disaster preparedness, that needs to change, according to Casey Helgeson, associate research professor in the Earth and Environmental Systems Institute at Penn State.

title: Raman spectroscopy meets the sugar shack
summary: Tasting 250 maple syrup samples a day for six months can tire the palate of even the best-trained taster. But that's the job of the inspectors who sample about half of the 400,000 barrels graded every year by the Producteurs et productrices acéricoles du Québec (PPAQ). This step, however, slows down the entire marketing chain.

title: Once logging stops, recovery of Vietnam's tropical forests isn't guaranteed
summary: Deep in the jungle of central Vietnam, the heat is heavy, the mosquitoes are relentless and the terrain offers no easy paths. My colleagues and I don't hike on clear trails; we wade up riverbeds, stepping carefully over slippery rocks to access the thousands of trees we have been measuring for the last decade.

title: Remote sensing maps rubber yields on Hainan Island
summary: A new study has developed a method to estimate rubber yields across Hainan Island, one of China's main natural rubber–producing regions. Using high-resolution remote sensing data, meteorological data and a limited set of field measurements, the team mapped annual dry rubber yields from 2021 to 2025.

title: Engineers reveal the interlayer elastic limits of van der Waals crystals
summary: A research team led by Professor Yang Lu from the Department of Mechanical Engineering in the Faculty of Engineering at The University of Hong Kong (HKU), in collaboration with Tsinghua University, has measured the interlayer elastic limits of graphite and hexagonal boron nitride, two representative van der Waals crystals, and revealed the physical mechanism that sets them. The work is published in the journal Nature Communications.

title: Roller-coaster flight reveals hidden electricity in clouds
summary: Measuring the electric charge in widespread, dull gray clouds could help scientists better understand droplets within them, a new study suggests.

title: Satellite maps reveal sinking land could worsen flooding across Africa's coastal cities by 2050
summary: Sinking land is widespread across major African coastal cities, according to a new Virginia Tech–led study published Nov. 27 in Science Advances.

title: A small galaxy's giant dark matter core challenges the standard cosmological model
summary: New findings show that a nearby dwarf galaxy, UGCA 320, may challenge some predictions of the widely accepted cosmological model of the universe. By combining observations from the MUSE instrument with radio measurements from the MeerKAT telescope, astronomers have found that it hosts an unusually large dark matter core. The paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Nov. 11.

title: New soil test could help farmers avoid costly crop damage
summary: Herbicides are essential for controlling weeds, but chemicals remaining in the soil after application can damage crops planted in subsequent seasons, particularly during dry conditions.

title: Can storybook characters teach children about perseverance?
summary: Many storybooks incorporate messages about not giving up when faced with a challenge—something that perhaps isn't surprising given that perseverance is an important factor for learning and long-term success.

title: Strawberries, cucumbers and lemon basil show promise for future moon and Mars menus
summary: As NASA prepares for future missions to the moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition and variety far from Earth. Such crop variety can help with menus in deep space, something top of mind this week as the nation celebrates Thanksgiving.

title: Why a warmer atmosphere doesn't guarantee more water in rivers
summary: Austria experienced an exceptional drought in 2026. From the start of the year until the end of October, rainfall was around a third lower than the long-term average. The consequences are low river flows and groundwater levels. But how is water availability linked to global warming? Shouldn't a warmer atmosphere, which can hold more water vapor, also lead to more rainfall?

title: Winner takes it all? Study highlights rise of zero-sum politics
summary: A growing tendency to view politics as a battle in which one group can only succeed at another's expense could be slowing economic growth and eroding support for Western democracies, according to new research by King's College London academics.

title: The world is experiencing a string of abnormally hot days—and records are being shattered
summary: We're becoming used to seeing records being broken whenever we look at data telling us about Earth's climate. Whether it's the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, heat in the ocean or shrinking sea ice around the poles, the signs of human-caused climate change are all around us.
